progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From b09: biotechnology's definition; the four kinds of change (a process used, the parents chosen, DNA copied, DNA inserted or edited); Bt cotton carries a gene from a soil bacterium and makes a protein against caterpillars; gene editing changes a chosen stretch of DNA. From Year 11 and b08: natural selection (individuals with favoured alleles survive and pass them on); gene pools and allele frequency. From Module 5 (B9 and B10): dominant and recessive alleles. From bio-m5-b06a: bacteria carry plasmids; antibiotic resistance genes can sit on plasmids. Not assumed: stakeholder, refuge, ethical judgement structure, the three kinds of question, the cases themselves.
progression.startsWith: Introduce a plant or animal biotechnology case. The video opens: Two biotechnologies.
progression.stopsAfter: explaining that a judgement needs a concrete benefit, a concrete harm or risk, and who gets each (stakeholders), not a list of pros and cons; judging Bt cotton in Australia (fewer insecticide sprays, benefiting growers, workers and beneficial insects; resistance by natural selection, managed with refuges; a licence fee to the trait owner; a monoculture remains), with a conditional verdict; explaining the hornless dairy cattle case (painful dehorning avoided by editing in a naturally occurring dominant hornless allele) and why the later discovery of inserted bacterial DNA shows that outcomes must be checked; explaining what animal cases add (the animal's own welfare, embryos and surrogates used, objections in principle); sorting objections into consequences (evidence can answer), distribution (policy decides) and principle (evidence cannot settle); applying this to an unseen Golden Rice item and an unseen AquAdvantage salmon evaluation with a verdict.
progression.nextLesson: where biotechnology might go in the future, and which benefits are plausible (route entry bio-m6-b11).

teaching.task: A cotton plant that poisons caterpillars and a bull edited so his calves grow no horns: both work, but how should we judge plant and animal biotechnology, and what does an animal case add?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why "it works" is not a judgement (benefits and harms fall on different groups, 2); why Bt cotton cuts spraying (the plant makes its own protein against caterpillars, 3); why resistance is a risk (resistant caterpillars survive and pass on their alleles, 4); why refuges help (susceptible caterpillars breed with resistant ones, keeping resistance alleles rare, 4); why the verdict needs a condition (the benefit lasts only while resistance is managed, 5); why edited cattle help welfare (no painful dehorning, 6); why the plasmid finding matters (intended and actual outcomes can differ, and only checking shows it, 7); why animal cases differ (an animal can suffer, 8); why some objections survive any evidence (they are about principle, 9). Visible case: one board; lines show who gets each benefit and harm; caterpillars move between the Bt block and the refuge. Video advantage: the refuge mixing, the magnifier finding the amber insert, chips dropping into bins. Thinking opportunities: two unseen items. Reading load: at most about three bright text items; the attempt 2 card is the densest frame and is the task.
teaching.conversationalApproach: A caterpillar-resistant cotton and a gene-edited hornless dairy bull both work, so the question is how to judge them and what an animal case adds; a judgement needs a concrete benefit, a concrete harm or risk, and who gets each (stakeholders), built on one judging board; Bt cotton in Australia is judged from fewer sprays, resistance managed by refuges and the licence fee to a conditional verdict; the hornless cattle case puts welfare on the benefit side, and the later discovery of inserted bacterial DNA shows that outcomes must be checked; objections then sort into consequences, distribution and principle. Two exam questions (Golden Rice, AquAdvantage salmon) follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Two biotechnologies. A cotton plant that makes its own protein against caterpillars. And a dairy bull whose DNA was edited so his calves would be born without horns. Both work. But working isn't the same as being a good idea. So how should we judge plant and animal biotechnology, and why does an animal case need something extra?
teaching.understandingCheck: 11a is an identify-and-explain item on Golden Rice: identify one group that could benefit and one concern; explain why evidence that it is safe to eat would not settle every objection. It tests the stakeholder lens and scene 9's three kinds of question. 11c is an evaluate item on AquAdvantage salmon: refer to a benefit, a risk and the groups affected, and reach a judgement. It tests the full route stop on a new animal case. Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; the full card stays on screen during and after the countdown. Each feedback is brief (about 25 to 30 s): answer, key reason, the givens underlined in the question strip as they are used, one crossed-out classic mistake. No givens card.
teaching.curriculumScope: B6-IQ2-01: "investigate the uses and applications of biotechnology (past, present and future), including: (ACSBL087)", with the listed sub-point this video carries: "analysing the social implications and ethical uses of biotechnology, including plant and animal examples". The other sub-points ("researching future directions ...", "evaluating the potential benefits for society ...", "evaluating the changes to the Earth's biodiversity ...") are b11 to b13. The verbs: "analysing" is carried by scene 9 (sorting objections into kinds) and attempt 1 (b); HSC questions on this sub-point use "evaluate", "assess" and "discuss" (`../research/question-types-bio-m6.md`), so attempt 2 asks for an evaluation with a verdict (what-markers-reward: "Evaluate ... reach a supported judgement"). Update the ledger row's sub-point coverage when this design passes review.

design.visualSystem: One judging board throughout: three columns, "benefit", "harm or risk", "who", with a case plate pinned at the top. Each entry is a short chip (two to six words) with a small stakeholder icon (coded, never people: a tractor outline for growers, a spray-can outline for farm workers' exposure, a bee outline for beneficial insects, a building outline for the seed company, a field-strip icon for ecosystems, an animal plate thumbnail for the animal). Lines join each benefit and each harm to its "who" chip, so the distribution is visible. The plant case (scenes 3 to 5) uses `m6-bt-cotton-v1.png` and the new `m6-helicoverpa-larva-boll-v1.png`, a coded spray-count bar ("before" against "after"), and a coded field map with a Bt block and a non-Bt refuge strip, in which caterpillar glyphs (open for susceptible, filled for resistant) move and breed. The animal case (scenes 6 to 8) uses the new `m6-dairy-calf-horn-buds-v1.png` and `b3b-dairy-bull-side-v1.png` (a hornless black-and-white dairy bull, labelled in code "a hornless dairy bull"; it is an ordinary bull plate, not the edited bull), a coded `SlimStrand` with the hornless allele as a cream band and, in scene 7, an amber inserted segment carrying two small "antibiotic resistance gene" bands, with `m6-bacterium-plasmid-v1.png` small as the source. Scene 9 has three question bins ("consequences", "distribution", "principle") into which earlier chips drop. Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): at most about three bright text items at once besides small grey icon labels; each chip dims once the next is placed; the board resets between the two cases.
design.transitionPlan: The cotton and bull plates open the hook with a works-not-justified line; the judging board draws its three columns and stakeholder icons; for Bt cotton the spray bars, refuge field with moving caterpillar glyphs and chips join to their groups one at a time before the verdict bar writes; the board resets for the hornless cattle, the DNA strip takes the cream hornless band and then, under the magnifier, the amber inserted segment; a welfare column slides in for the animal case; the chips drop into three question bins; the checklist writes large; each attempt clears the board and its feedback underlines the card as the small board fills; the decision rule chips and next chip close; scene crossfade with settle.
